Istanbul’s location between Europe and Asia has always given it particular strategic and economic importance, especially as it lies on the only sea route that connects the Black Sea with the Mediterranean. By the early 20th century, it was the Ottoman world’s largest port city.

The Sultan Valide Mosque dominates the port of Eminönü on the Golden Horn. Eminönü became a prosperous port in the Ottoman period due to its lively trade with the West. In the wake of industrialisation, its importance was further enhanced by the Galata Bridge, the arrival of steamships, the introduction of electricity and the railway, with the terminal for the Orient Express built close by at the Sirkeci Station.

During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed the appearance of Istanbul port. The construction of Galata Pier began in 1892 and was completed in 1900. Two warehouses were built in 1910 and three more added in 1928. From 1925 onwards, the port authority started to provide all the necessary logistic support to visiting ships, including water and coal, loading and unloading, maritime pilotage and marine salvage services.

Ports could hold not only commercial but also military significance. From the late 1700s, Sebastopol was the base of the Imperial Russian Black Sea fleet and a crucial strategic factor in the tsars’ long-held dream of gaining access to the Mediterranean. Badly damaged in the 1850s Crimean war, it nevertheless has served as a Russian naval base to this day.

The prosperous cosmopolitan port city of Smyrna (modern Izmir) owed as much to the tolerant Tanzimat reforms of the Ottoman empire as it did to its geographic location. Shortly after this scene was recorded, Smyrna was transformed into an industrialised harbour welcoming steamships and railways.

From the mid-19th century, the overwhelming majority of British exports to the Middle East arrived through the four major western Anatolian ports of Smyrna (modern Izmir), Trabzon, Samsun and Mersin. As a result, these cities grew rapidly: the population of Smyrna tripled.

Arab port cities increased dramatically in importance late in the 19th century. The value of commercial goods handled by the seven principal ports of Syria and Palestine, including Jaffa, rose 68 per cent between the 1880s and 1913.

In 1887, the Ottoman authorities granted the concession to modernise the port of Beirut to the Ottoman–European Compagnie du Port, des Quais et des Entrepots de Beyrouth. As a result Beirut’s population gradually soared from 10,000 in 1800 to around 150,000 in 1914.
In the early 1900s, the port of Aqaba gained considerable importance after the construction of the Hijaz railway, which connected it to both Damascus and the Holy City of Medina.

From the later 18th century onwards, the ancient port city of Alexandria evolved into a very important international centre for trade and shipping, not least due to its geographic location, giving access to the Mediterranean and overland to the Red Sea. Unfortunately, for the same reasons, it was also a prized asset for European powers and had to witness both Napoleon’s invasion in 1798 and that of the British in 1882.

The port of Tunis, La Goulette, was developed into a state-of-the-art facility in the late 19th century. It served for export and import, passenger transport, fishing and as an industrial centre, particularly after coastal train and tram lines ran to its northern suburbs.

Algiers had long been an important Mediterranean port. After the French invasion of 1830, it was rapidly developed and peopled by foreigners coming in from north of the Mediterranean. By the early 20th century, the majority of Algiers’ residents were Europeans.

Throughout the 19th century, Casablanca was a moderate port focused on the export of wool to and import of tea from the UK. In 1904, at the initiative of Sultan Mulay ‘Abd al-Aziz, the authorities commissioned the French Compagnie Marocaine to develop the port.

A crucial entrepôt for the India trade, the British annexed Aden in 1839 and made it a free port in 1850. After the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, Aden’s strategic importance increased greatly as the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden became ever busier and vital trade routes to the East.

From their fort in the port town of Sharjah, the Al-Qawasim dynasty oversaw an increasingly prosperous pearling trade in the 19th century. Sharjah soon turned into the pre-eminent economic hub on the Arab side of the Gulf coast. At the same time, throughout the 19th century and until the early 1900s, Sharjah, and Ras al-Khaimah remained the only two custom posts on that side of the Gulf.

Up to the early 19th century, al-Zubarah, on the west coast of Qatar, was an important regional centre for the Gulf pearl trade. Its commercial success attracted the attention of other Gulf powers, and after several attacks the town was eventually burnt down in 1811, never to recover. A small pearl fishing community continued to live in al-Zubarah, but eventually the site was abandoned.

In 1880, the French Péreire brothers’ Compagnie Générale Transatlantique established itself in North Africa and started an important steamship service involving 12 vessels, including the *Ville de Rome*, out of Marseille.

Livorno’s fortunes always rose and fell according to the economic politics and rivalries of European powers. Napoleon occupied it twice to destroy the British hold on the port and ruin its chances of competing with the French port of Marseille. Its fortunes returned in the 19th century, with increasing industrialisation and the establishment of the Orlando shipyards in 1865.

Many European ports trading with the Ottoman Empire were situated along the Danube. Constanţa harbour was built by a British company in 1857. In 1896, the Romanian state entrusted the port’s modernisation to a French company, but the project stalled because of disagreements. In 1899, under the direction of the Romanian engineer Anghel Saligny, and with the help of engineers I.B. Cantacuzino, Gh. Duca, M. Râmniceanu and C. Casimir, the work was completed.

In the 19th century, Marseille’s economy was determined by its role as France’s “Gate to the Orient”, linking it with its North African colonies and – via the Suez canal – economic interests further afield. The original trading port at Marseille was later replaced by the Port de la Joliette.

In the 19th century, Marseille’s economy was determined by its role as France’s “Gate to the Orient”, linking it with its North African colonies and – via the Suez canal – economic interests further afield. The original trading port at Marseille was later replaced by the Port de la Joliette.

In the 19th century, Marseille’s economy was determined by its role as France’s “Gate to the Orient”, linking it with its North African colonies and – via the Suez canal – economic interests further afield. The original trading port at Marseille was later replaced by the Port de la Joliette.

The biggest Palestinian cotton growing and processing centres were Acre during the 19th century and later the hill region Jabal Nablus, both situated in the north of Palestine. The raw cotton and the cotton yarn they produced were imported mainly by France for its textile industry.

In the 19th century the cultivation of cotton was expanded in the northern districts of Palestine (the territory of present-day Israel and Palestine, which was then part of the Ottoman Empire). Cotton became the main European import from the region, but by the 1870s the lack of industrialisation led to a decline of cotton production and trade.

According to this document, in 1868 Venice imported from Egypt 377,200kg of raw cotton. In the 19th century, cotton became Egypt’s leading export after French textile engineer Louis Alexis Jumel, who had been hired by Viceroy Muhammad ‘Ali to manage a textile factory in Cairo, developed a new type of cotton. With the support of Muhammad ‘Ali, the extensive cultivation of Jumel long-staple cotton began in the 1820s.

Silk became in the 19th century the main agricultural produce of Mount Lebanon, most of it being exported to France. In 1841, three French entrepreneurs – Nicolas, Joseph and Antoine Fortuné Portalis – founded the first silk factory in Mount Lebanon, which was built in Btater, and European spinners were brought to teach the locals the European method of spinning silk threads.

In the 1840s, French silkworms were infected with a new disease called pébrine, which then spread to the rest of Europe and the Middle East, affecting both European and Arab and Ottoman silk industries. In 1865, the French government assigned chemist Louis Pasteur to find the cause of the disease. After studying pébrine for five years, Pasteur discovered a cure that stopped the epidemics in all regions it had reached.

In the 19th century, tobacco grown in Latakia (north-east Syria), which was considered the best produced in the province, was especially favoured by the British. The production and export of tobacco was a state monopoly in the Ottoman Empire, but the difficult economic situation that the empire was dealing with in the late 19th century led to the ceding of tobacco revenues to a consortium of three European-owned banks.

Oriental water pipes called *huqqa*s (from Persian for “coconut” because they used to be made from coconut shells) or *narghiles*s (in Turkish) are thought to have originated in India, from where they spread to Iran and reached the Ottoman Empire in the 17th century. They later became popular in the Balkans too.

Pearl exports constituted the principal source of income for the Arab emirates on the western coast of the Arab-Persian Gulf until the beginning of the 20th century, when the Japanese discovered how to produce cultured pearls.

The economy of Sharjah was largely based until the 19th century on maritime trading with Africa and the Far East and on the building of traditional shipping vessels. But after the British, keen to maintain their monopoly on the trade routes to India, imposed their protectorate over the Arab sheikdoms in the Gulf region and destroyed most of their commercial vessels, Sharjah reoriented its economy to pearl fishing and trading.

Even under the British protectorate, pearl fishing was regulated in the Arab sheikdoms on the east coast of the Arabian Peninsula by the local authorities and was practised only by locals. Furthermore, the British government forbade the exploitation of pearl fisheries by British and foreign companies.

In the 19th century, Europeans also purchased from the Arab sheikdoms in the Gulf mother-of-pearl, the shiny layer inside some pearl shells, which was used in jewellery making and in decorating buttons, wooden furniture, weapons and liturgical objects.
Dhows, traditional wooden Arabian sailing vessels, could be of various types. Those generally used for pearl fishing were called *sambuk*.

Ever since the 16th century, the Regency of Algiers licensed the rights for fishing coral in its coastal waters to French companies. After the French Revolution of 1789, France decided to give up its monopoly over coral fishing in Algeria and so fishing rights also began to be granted to other Europeans, such as the British and the Italians.

Two years after the conquest of Algiers (1830), the French authorities established a set of rules for coral fishing in Algeria. Foreign companies were accepted but had to pay fees for fishing coral, while French boats were exempt from any taxes.

In 1852 a treaty was signed by Tunis and France, by which the latter granted France exclusive rights over the Tunisian coral fishery in exchange for the annual payment of a tax to the Tunisian government. This monopoly was preserved after Tunisia became a French protectorate, with the annual tax being paid instead into the French Treasury of the Finance Commission.

Until the 19th century, coffee was imported in the Middle East from Yemen. But after European powers began cultivating it in their colonies in the Caribbean, these became the main centres for the import of coffee by the Middle East.

In the 19th century, the consumption of Yemeni coffee was replaced in the Ottoman Empire with that of coffee brought in from the French and British colonies in the West Indies, which had lower costs due to the use of slave labour. For the port of Smyrna, coffee was one of the principal imported products.

After Algeria became a French colony, most of its coffee was imported from the West Indian colonies of France, whose commercial vessels paid lower custom duties than vessels from other countries for coffee shipments.

In North Africa, as in the Middle East, coffee was imported in the 19th century from European colonies in the West Indies. According to Thomas MacGill, a Scottish merchant who visited Tunisia in 1811, by then Tunisians were already using much more coffee from Martinique, one of France’s West Indian colonies, than from Yemen.

Although Yemen lost supremacy in the coffee trade because of coffee produced in the West Indies and commercialised by the British and the French, exports of Yemeni coffee to Europe did not completely cease thanks to its good quality, which had made it famous. And it was still consumed within the Arabian Peninsula, where inhabitants used a traditional coffee pot (*dallah*) to prepare it.

Until they obtained their independence in the 19th century, the south-eastern European countries that were under Ottoman suzerainty had to provide the empire with agricultural produce. In the Romanian countries, sheep, and derivative products (wool, lambskin, cheese, meat and tallow), were primarily exported to the Ottoman Empire until Wallachia and Moldavia were granted freedom of commerce through the Treaty of Edirne (1829).

Camel hair was imported by European states in the 19th century from the Middle East and North Africa, with Turkey, Algeria and Egypt being the main exporters. Camel hair was used, for example, to make straps, hats and paint brushes.

Although sugar cane grew in the Middle East and North Africa, refined sugar was imported from France and Britain, which obtained sugar from their West Indian colonies. In Egypt, however, during the reigns of Muhammad ‘Ali and his grandson Isma‘il Pasha, the cultivation of sugar was extended and sugar refineries were founded (the first in 1818 by an Englishman). By the late 19th century, Egypt produced enough sugar to become an exporter of raw and refined sugar.

On the African continent there were several caravan routes that connected southern and central Africa with the Maghreb by crossing the Sahara, which separates these areas. Some of the trans-Saharan trade routes headed to ports situated on the Atlantic or Mediterranean coasts of North Africa, which were trading hubs important for the commerce with Europe.

The territory of Morocco was crossed by western trans-Saharan caravan routes, some of which led to ports that played an important role in the commercial exchanges with Europe, such as Tetouan, Rabat and Casablanca.

Cities that were situated along caravan routes were usually important commercial centres where a thriving trade took place, as merchants travelling through them with caravans would sell goods they had purchased on their way there and buy local ones.

The main caravan routes used in the Balkans for the trade with the Ottoman Empire all led to Istanbul. Two of the most important were ancient roads that had been built by the Romans. One (Via Militaris, 1st century AD) headed to Istanbul by passing through Belgrade, Nish, Sofia, Plovdiv and Edirne. The other (Via Egnatia, 2nd century BC) passed through Dyrrachium, Edessa, Pella, Thessaloniki and Edirne.

In 1863 a carriage road was built between Damascus and Beirut by a French company under Ottoman jurisdiction (Compagnie Impériale Ottoman de la Route de Beyrouth à Damas). This had a positive influence on silk exports to France. Silk was transported by land to the port of Beirut and then by sea to Marseille.

Constanţa–Cernavodă, the first railway in the European part of the Ottoman Empire, was built to facilitate the transportation of exportable products, especially cereals, to the Black Sea port of Constanţa, from where they were shipped to Istanbul.

A railway connecting Damascus to the Mediterranean port of Beirut was built between 1891 and 1895 by the Société des Chemins de fer Ottomans économiques de Beyrouth-Damas-Hauran, which had been granted a concession from the Ottoman authorities. By making it easier to transport merchandise to Beirut, from where it was sent by sea to Europe, the construction of the railway favoured trade relations with Europe.

Aleppo–Beirut used to be one of the major Levantine routes for caravan trade. At the beginning of the 20th century the two cities were connected by a railway that was opened in 1906 and in time the caravans’ role in transporting commodities by land was taken over by trains.
The Aswan–Luxor railway, which was inaugurated in 1926–27, was part of the railway system that connected the inland of Egypt with the Mediterranean coast through the Nile valley.

This later Ottoman silver coin still reflects aspects – in part European-inspired – of the classic currency designs maintained by the empire over centuries. It was minted in Constantinople in AH 1327 / AD 1909 and includes the *tughra* (imperial monogram) and blessings relating to Sultan Muhammad V.

In the 18th and early 19th centuries, the official imperial coinage of the Ottoman Empire was legal tender in all of its provinces, including the Balkans. The circulation of Ottoman coins dominated the money markets in Romania, Moldavia and Wallachia.

In the 19th century, several regions of the Ottoman Empire used coinage as a symbol of defiance against its overlordship. In Romania, a new monetary law in 1867 led to the first issue of national coins for the United Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia without any reference to Ottoman sovereignty.

This copper coin was minted in the holy city of Mecca in AH 1334 / AD 1915. At the time, Mecca was also the capital of the Hashemite Arab government under Sharif Husayn ibn ‘Ali, whose struggle against Ottoman rule was supported by the UK and rewarded with his recognition as King of the Hijaz from 1917 to 1924.

In 1834 a governmental decree introduced the Egyptian pound (gineh) as the main currency unit. Exchange rates against European currencies circulating in Egypt were fixed, with the Egyptian pound pegged to the British pound sterling. Bank notes were issued from 1899.

In 1916 Egypt introduced a range of new base metal and gold coins in addition to the existing silver denominations. The reform came in the wake of Britain’s declaring Egypt its protectorate at the start of World War I to ensure a crucial economic, financial as well as political hold over the country.

In North Africa, too, currency reforms eventually led to the introduction of European-style coins and bank notes, particularly after France tightened its grip on the region with the occupation of Algeria in 1830 and Tunisia in 1881. This banknote was issued by the Bank of Algeria, the only bank authorised to issue banknotes in Tunisia at the time.

Between the 19th and early 20th centuries, Middle Eastern and North African money was increasingly designed and produced in Europe, even if their designs hardly betray this fact. Moroccan coins like these were minted in Berlin, London or Birmingham.

Between the 19th and early 20th centuries, Middle Eastern and North African money was increasingly designed and produced in Europe, even if their designs hardly betray this fact. Moroccan coins like these were minted in Berlin, London or Birmingham.

First minted in 1741, the Austrian Maria Theresia thaler (or dollar) played a key role in Middle Eastern trade. It was declared an official trade coinage in 1857, one year before it ceased to be legal tender in Austria itself. In the Arabian Peninsula, it remained popular into the 20th century due to its high silver content.

An estimated 400 million Maria Theresa thalers were produced in several European mints and even one Indian mint between 1780 and the early 20th century. From Mediterranean ports, they made their way to Ottoman and Arab lands, including those bordering the Red Sea and the Arab-Persian Gulf.

In the Middle East as well as across the Red and Arabian seas, the Arab-Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean, the Maria Theresa thaler was highly regarded and used in all aspects of life, from dowry payments and jewellery to economic transactions. Muslim pilgrims, too, favoured this internationally accepted coin.

This thaler with the effigy of the Austrian Emperor Francis I was countersigned in the Hijaz around 1920. Habsburg silver currency, most commonly the Maria Theresa coin, was the most popular throughout the region and used in large quantities to pay for essential commodities.

British Indian rupees were first used in the Gulf from the mid-19th century. The currency began circulating in the region as a result of the pearl trade between local and Indian merchants. The rupee continued as the Trucial States’ main currency until 1966.

Copper coins like this one, known as Mardhouf al-Qawasim, were minted in Lanja in the Arabian Gulf in AH 1247 / AD 1831. They were used in regions ruled by the Qawasim family at the time, including Sharjah, Ras al-Khaimah, Kalba, Khor Fakkan and Diba.

During the 19th century, the most profitable period for the export to Europe of cotton cultivated in Anatolia, the Levant (north Palestine, north Syria) and Egypt was the 1860s, when because of the American Civil War (1861–65) European imports of American cotton were cut off.

Although silk had been produced in Europe since the 11th century, with Italy, France and the UK being the main European silk centres, by the 19th century internal supplies were not sufficient to meet the demands of the growing French silk industry. Therefore, silk was brought in from the Middle East, where the biggest silk producer was the Levant.

Most of the pearls imported into Western Europe came in the 19th century from the Arab sheikdoms in the Gulf region, whose coastal waters were rich in pearls and where pearl fishing was the main economic activity. Pearl fisheries were found on the Arabian coast of the Red Sea too, from where pearls were exported to Europe via Alexandria, while those from the Gulf sheikdoms were first sent to Bombay in India and then re-exported worldwide.

The drinking of coffee, discovered by the Arabs, was introduced in the 16th century in the Ottoman Empire, from where it spread to Europe. Until the 18th century, Yemen held the monopoly on coffee production and exports. But it lost this pre-eminence after European powers started to grow coffee in their West Indian and American colonies and became by the 19th century the main coffee exporters into Europe, the Middle East and North Africa.

The greatest share of European finished goods imported into the Arab and Ottoman world was represented in the 19th century by woollen, silk and cotton cloths. These were purchased mainly from the UK, France and Italy, where the technical innovations of the Industrial Revolution, especially the development of spinning machinery, increased production and lowered its costs.

In the 19th century, European technological superiority in terms of military equipment, combined with the modernisation of armies in the Arab and Ottoman world under the influence of Western European trends, led to a constant import of European firearms.

In the 19th century, the influx of imported European finished goods into the Arab and Ottoman markets led to the decline of the local crafts that produced equivalent items. Although this did not mean the disappearance of traditional occupations, it diminished their importance within local economies.

In the later 19th century, Damascus was one of the Middle Eastern cities with increasing political and economic significance. A key hub for trans-desert and intra-regional trade, pilgrimage caravans and – later – the Hijaz railway, its urban fabric was steadily refashioned to reflect its status as a modern administrative centre of the late Ottoman empire.

In the later 19th century, Damascus was one of the Middle Eastern cities with increasing political and economic significance. A key hub for trans-desert and intra-regional trade, pilgrimage caravans and, later, the Hijaz railway, its urban fabric was steadily refashioned to reflect its status as a modern administrative centre of the late Ottoman empire, its Dar al-Baladiyya a municipal symbol of Ottoman reform.

Unlike other 19th-century trade hubs, Damascus was spared the often destructive processes of urban Occidentalisation. Instead, traditional houses such as Bayt Niyadu, the property of a wealthy member of the Jewish business and finance community, were refurbished, modernised and provided with electricity.

Although living inland in both Damascus and Aleppo, members of the Jewish Lisbona family upheld wide trading networks, and some family members emigrated to Manchester in the later 19th century to run a shipping business.

In the 19th century, Cairo was one of the most crucial economic, commercial and political hubs in the Southern Mediterranean. Rapid modernisation, with wide avenues, trams and railways as well as modern communications, was aimed at accelerating the city’s prosperity. The enormous debts incurred as a result, however, led to increasing financial and political interference by European powers, culminating in the British invasion of Egypt in 1882.

In the 19th century, London became the largest port and city in the world, counting 6 million citizens from the United Kingdom, Europe and all over the world in its midst. Its port handled 8 million tons of goods in 1880, while its city exerted powerful financial and political influence at home and abroad.

After much upheaval in the early 19th century, Paris underwent extensive modernisation under Napoleon III (1852–70). However, the city only became an international economic, commercial and financial centre in the wake of its 1889 Exposition Universelle, world famous for the spectacular Eiffel Tower, the tallest structure in the world at the time.

Relatively insignificant until 1871, Berlin rapidly developed into an internationally important metropolis by 1914. Industry and infrastructure expanded particularly after the receipt of 5 billion francs in French war reparations, which financed trade, industrial investment and the establishment of financial institutions. But success also had a dark side: many citizens and immigrants suffered from abject poverty and disease.

The imperial capital of the vast Austro-Hungarian empire, Vienna was the political, economic and cultural hub of Central Europe. A steady flow of ethnically and religiously diverse migrants between 1870 and 1900 boosted the city’s economic development but also created tensions, as many suffered from exploitative working conditions and sought political organisation to defend their rights.

Bucharest’s fortunes increased after Romania’s independence in 1877. The city was modernised, its economic opportunities expanding accordingly. Mentioned in documents since the 16th century, this street connected the city centre with its east side. An annual trade fair was held here. As the fair grew, the street was extended, with many shops, inns, restaurants and workshops on either side.

In 1826 the fez, worn in the Greek islands and already in use among North African Muslims, replaced the turban in Ottoman army uniforms, becoming in 1829 compulsory for male civilians too. Fezzes were imported from Austro-Hungary until 1908, when its annexation of Bosnia-Herzegovina triggered an Ottoman boycott of Austrian goods. In 1925 wearing a fez was forbidden by Kemal Ataturk (first President of the Turkish Republic) because fezzes were considered a reminder of the old regime.

Apart from the garments and cloths it imported from Western Europe, Tunisia also purchased gold and silver threads, as well as articles of passementerie, which were used in the ornamentation of traditional clothes.

Gold and silk threads were imported by Tunisia, as well as by Algeria, mostly from Lyon, a French city famous for its production of textile gildings (*dorures*) and articles of passementerie until the 1920s.
In the 19th century, gold thread, which was used in adorning traditional garments, was imported by Algeria from Europe, especially from Lyon.

In 1914 the Singer Company, an American manufacturer of sewing machines, established an Italian subsidiary in Milan. As proved by this advertisement, Singer sewing machines produced in Italy were also sold in Libya, which had become an Italian colony in 1912.

In the late 19th century, as Moroccan Sultan Hasan I took measures to increase the military capacity of his sultanate, he also deemed it necessary to modernise the army’s weaponry. Firearms and artillery were therefore purchased from Western Europe, mostly from the UK and France, but from other countries too.

For the manufacturing of swords, blades were imported in 19th-century Morocco from Syria, but also from Toledo, where blades whose steel was considered comparable in quality to Damascus steel were produced by the Royal Manufactory built in 1780 outside the city in the valley of the river Tagus.

In the 19th century, Western European firearms represented one of the prime European imports of the Arab Emirates on the western coast of the Gulf. At the same time, guns were produced locally based on European models.

Even though flintlocks had been manufactured in the Ottoman Empire since the end of the 16th century, three centuries later the Ottoman army was being equipped with handguns imported from Western Europe, whose weapons industry was significantly more advanced than the Ottoman one.

As well as importing European finished goods, in the Arab and Ottoman world there were attempts to modernise local industries by using European technology and specialists. In 1885 Moroccan Sultan Mulay al-Hasan founded a weapons factory in Fez, near the royal palace. Called by the inhabitants *makina*, from the French word *machine*, the factory was equipped with Italian machinery. An Italian officer and two mechanics were hired to administrate it, while the labourers were local ironsmiths.

The imperial tile factory in Istanbul, which produced high-quality European-style ceramics for the Ottoman market, was built following the plans of Italian architect Raimondo Tommaso D’Aronco. It functioned between 1895 and 1936, using technology similar to that found in the French porcelain factory of Sèvres and employing both Turkish and European artisans.

The porcelains produced by the Yıldız factory with local materials and traditional Turkish designs, but using European techniques, were destined for the Turkish court and upper classes, in an attempt to reduce ceramics imports from Europe.

In the 19th century, Italians were Egypt’s main foreign community after the Greek one. Some Italians had set up successful businesses such as the furniture factory of Giuseppe Parvis, who settled in Cairo in 1859 and whose products were very popular with wealthy Egyptians.
In the 19th century, members of the Moroccan upper classes purchased items of furniture made in Western Europe. Italian producers were among the most appreciated.

At the beginning of the 20th century, Morocco’s war fleet comprised a cruiser and two troopships. The cruiser, *Bascir*, was bought from Italy in 1890 and its first captain and mechanical engineers were Europeans.

The yacht *Makook III*, commissioned in 1911 by the Khedive of Egypt from the Fratelli Orlando naval shipyard in Livorno, was the second ship that this Italian company built for a North African state after the cruiser *Bascir*, which it sold to the Sultan of Morocco in 1890.

After Algeria became a French colony, its large cork oak forests began to supply France’s cork factories while at the same time French entrepreneurs engaged in the local production of Algerian handmade corks, much appreciated in Europe for their quality. To increase production, in the second half of the 19th century the French brought to Algeria a machine for cutting corks already in use in Europe, which soon replaced traditional cork making.

Through the Strait of Gibraltar, which connects the Mediterranean to the Atlantic, the ships of European countries bordering the Atlantic could enter the Mediterranean and trade with Anatolian, Levantine and North African lands. At the same time, the Strait offered trading vessels of European Mediterranean states access to the Atlantic in order to circumnavigate Africa and reach the Red Sea and the Arab-Persian Gulf.
In 1869 the opening of the Suez Canal, which was built to unite the Mediterranean and the Red Seas, marked the inauguration of a shorter trade route between Europe and the Arabian Peninsula.

Since the discovery of the trade route to India in the 15th century, Europeans reached the Arabian Peninsula by circumnavigating Africa. This changed in the late 19th century when the Suez Canal made it possible for ships to sail from the Mediterranean directly into the Red Sea.

The legal status of the Suez Canal was established through the convention of Constantinople (signed on 29 October 1888 by Austro-Hungary, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Russia, the Ottoman Empire and the UK), according to which the canal was to be open in times of peace for all commercial vessels.

The construction of the Suez Canal was not a 19th-century idea, but actually represented the re-establishment of an ancient trade route between Europe and Asia. The first canal to connect the Mediterranean and Red seas had been built by Egyptian pharaoh Necoh II in the 7th century BC, but was blocked by the Abbasid caliph Al-Mansur in the late 8th century AD.

Whereas in the past it held a marginal position, the Red Sea became an important waterway for commerce between Europe and the Arab and Ottoman world starting from the second half of the 19th century when the construction of the Suez Canal linked it to the Mediterranean.

The Gulf of Aden became in the late 19th century part of the new trade route created between Europe and the Arabian Peninsula through the construction of the Suez Canal. After crossing the canal and accessing the Red Sea from the Mediterranean, ships sailed the Gulf of Aden to enter the Arabian Sea and then the Indian Ocean.

The Black Sea, whose western shore connected the Ottoman Empire with its European possessions, was for centuries under the control of the Ottomans and no foreign vessels were allowed to sail or trade on it. This monopoly was lost in the late 18th century when Russia was granted navigational rights after the Russian-Ottoman war of 1768–74. Later, the Treaty of Edirne (1829) gave the same rights to all European countries at peace with the Empire.

Trade and transportation on the Danube – a major river route on which commodities from the Empire’s Balkan possessions were transported to Black Sea ports to be shipped to Istanbul – were controlled by the Ottomans since the 16th century. This lasted until after the Crimean War when the peace Treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March 1856 by France, the UK, Russia, the Ottoman Empire, Austria, Prussia and Sardinia, introduced free navigation on the Danube.

The discovery of steam power had a positive impact on river transportation and implicitly on commerce in the Middle East. This is because before the appearance of steamships important river routes such as the Euphrates or the Tigris could only be sailed downstream, while from the 19th century merchandise could be transported upstream too.

In the later 19th century, the London Stock Exchange became the world’s most powerful financial centre. By 1914, one-third of the public capital available to investors anywhere in the world was listed and traded on the London Stock Exchange. Other European powers tried to establish rival institutions, but none could match it in scale, scope or available resources.

Alongside powerful financial centres such as London and Amsterdam, Paris also provided considerable investment capital for economic and other projects across the Southern Mediterranean. Many brokers at the Paris Stock Exchange dealt in shares and bonds related to reformist government schemes.

Unlike its main rivals in London and Paris, the Berlin Stock Exchange, founded in 1865, had few dealings with the southern Mediterranean, but specialised mainly in inter-European and American investment markets.

Founded in 1771, the Vienna Stock Exchange crashed in 1873 in the wake of a global economic crisis that ushered in the Long Depression that was to last until 1896. Southern Mediterranean countries suffered during this period too: foreign trade declined, trade terms deteriorated and growing European interference in the region’s financial affairs led to increasing indebtedness and foreign credit.

The greatest economic world power up to the 17th century, Portugal faced grave challenges throughout the 1800s. Setting its economic hopes on South America and Africa rather than the Middle East, it played a key role in the European powers’ 1885 agreement to carve up Africa among themselves for colonialisation and economic exploitation.

The Alexandria Stock Exchange was opened in 1883, followed in 1903 by the one in Cairo. Initially focused exclusively on transactions relating to the cotton trade with Europe, the exchange soon became the focus of the city’s entire financial community.

The Ottoman (later Imperial Ottoman) Bank was established in Istanbul in 1856. Sustained by British, French and some Ottoman capital, it functioned as the state’s bank in advancing credits, managing debt, issuing currency and overseeing the state’s budgets.

Following severe financial predicaments in the 1870s, Ottoman financial officials were increasingly forced to work under foreign financial control. Under the terms of the Ottoman Public Debt Administration established in 1881, thousands were instructed and managed by European financiers.

This archaeological notebook belonged to Robert Hamilton Lang, the Scottish manager of the Imperial Ottoman Bank in Larnaca, Cyprus, between 1863 and 1872. He later held other IOB posts in Alexandria, Romania and Constantinople, where he became director general of the bank in 1875.

The foundation of the State Bank of Morocco came in the wake of the Algeciras Conference in 1906, during which European powers and the USA agreed on how to apportion control over the most crucial of Morocco’s political, economic and financial affairs. The State Bank gave credit, issued currency and oversaw state finance.

While powerful stock exchanges and national banks controlled major financial transactions in the later 19th and early 20th centuries, many ordinary people and small and medium-scale businesses still relied on the services of traditional moneylenders and private bankers. In many areas these remained the only reliable source for informal credit and funds for some time.

One of the most important trade routes for the commerce between Europe and the Arab and Ottoman world was the Mediterranean Sea, on which commodities were shipped to and from Western European ports and North African and Levantine ones.

The commerce of Europe with the Arabian Peninsula benefited from the construction of the Suez Canal, because by connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea the distance between the two geographical regions was drastically shortened and the duration of commercial transports was significantly reduced.

In North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, caravans remained the main method of transporting commodities overland well into the 19th century. In the Arab and Ottoman world goods were carried using camels, whereas in the Balkans horses, mules or donkeys were used.

In the second half of the 19th century the first railways began to be built in the Middle East, the Balkans and North Africa. As the railway system expanded, caravan trade gradually disappeared because carrying merchandise overland by train was more profitable since it allowed the transportation of larger quantities of products in less time.

Pera (also known as Galata) lies on Istanbul’s European side. Traditionally it was home to foreign merchants and European embassies. In the 19th century, it became Istanbul’s most Westernised area, with its diverse foreign communities opening modern schools, shops and cultural venues.

In 19th-century Cairo, European communities tended to live in the ‘Quarter of the Franks’ (*harat al franj*). At its heart lay a market and several European-style, glass-fronted shops owned by members of the various foreign communities resident in the city.

19th-century Tunis attracted many economic immigrants, particularly from France, the Italian islands and Malta. By the early 1900s, Tunis was home to huge French and Italian colonies, with half of its population foreign.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a cosmopolitan city in which a high percentage of non-Muslim communities lived and worked peacefully alongside their Muslim neighbours. Many inhabitants were Greeks, influential in economic as well as cultural and intellectual life.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, Smyrna (modern Izmir) was a cosmopolitan city in which a high percentage of non-Muslim communities lived and worked peacefully alongside their Muslim neighbours. Many of the best silversmiths active in the city were Greeks and Armenians.

Many non-Muslim Ottomans – Greeks, Armenians and Jews among them – worked as translators and employees of European merchants active in Middle Eastern ports and cities. This firman with the *tughra* (imperial monogram) of Sultan Mahmud II dated August/September 1819 legislates for such employees in Smyrna.

The commercial elite, whether local or foreign, played an active part in the political, social and cultural life of the cities they had settled in. From his residence in Alexandria, A.L. Benaki, for example, oversaw many important philanthropic projects for the benefit of the city’s community at large.

Many economic migrants from Italy, France, Greece and Malta went to North Africa in the later 19th century. Some came for specific business and set up or helped sustain successful enterprises in the trading ports and cities of the region.

Marius Scalesi was a poet born in Tunis in 1892 to parents of Italian-Maltese descent. A fascinating personality due to his complex, multifaceted identity, Scalesi is today considered one of the pioneers of North African poetry written in French.

Over centuries, Greeks were among the most widely dispersed, economically successful and best-integrated trading communities active throughout the Mediterranean region, the Near East and many parts of Europe. Wherever they settled, they combined a cosmopolitan lifestyle with a firm commitment to upholding their orthodox faith and communal traditions.

Greeks always played an important part in the economy of Egypt, be it as wealthy entrepreneurs based in Alexandria and Cairo or as small shop owners and financiers making a living in the countryside. Rather than living in foreign enclaves, many preferred to settle right at the heart of their host communities.
For centuries, Armenian communities played an important economic part in societies around the Mediterranean. In Istanbul, they were among the most influential and integrated commercial communities.

Southern European Jews had settled in many North African cities by the 19th century. This treaty asserts Tuscan jurisdiction and protection for Tuscan Jews in Tunisia. Many European powers insisted on similar treaties for religious minorities resident in Muslim lands both to ensure their safety and as covert opportunities to interfere in a country’s internal affairs.

Jews from many different geographic backgrounds formed an active and influential part of Istanbul’s urban population over many centuries. In the 19th century, Jewish financiers and merchants such as Abraham Salomon de Camondo (1781–1873), the patriarch of the mercantile Camondo family, worked closely with the Ottoman government and their communities, establishing workshops and schools such as the Camondo Institute.

Abraham Behor (1829–89) and Nisim Camondo (1892–1917), the grandsons of Abraham Salomon de Camondo, looked after the Camondo business interests in Paris after their families left Istanbul in 1869. Their descendants were to become important supporters and benefactors of the arts.
Binjamin Uziyel belonged to one of the influential Jewish families in Istanbul involved in finance, commerce, philanthropy and, indeed, politics.

Successful members of Jewish commercial communities, such as Raffaello Moreno and his brother Leon – whose family originated from Livorno – were often acknowledged by both their native and resident countries, a fact represented here by this Tunisian-Italian decoration.

Istanbul’s location between Europe and Asia has always given it particular strategic and economic importance, especially as it lies on the only sea route that connects the Black Sea with the Mediterranean. By the early 20th century, it was the Ottoman world’s largest port city.

This bustling market scene in Romania gives a good impression of traditional outdoor trading. Itinerant rural traders and peddlers offer their produce, poultry, animals and other wares from simple baskets, stalls or carts. Women played a crucial part in all aspects of trade, either at the forefront or behind the scenes.

In the 19th century, London became the largest port and city in the world, counting 6 million citizens from the United Kingdom, Europe and all over the world in its midst. Its port handled 8 million tons of goods in 1880, while its city exerted powerful, financial and political influence at home and abroad.

A traditional open-air market brought together individual traders selling their produce, crafts and animals. Some were based locally, others arrived regularly with trading caravans to sell staples or rare commodities from much further afield.

Women played a crucial part in all aspects of trade, either at the forefront or behind the scenes.

At markets, the weighing systems of commodities were set and regularly controlled by the state. These Romanian weighing units relied on Ottoman conventions, which were used in the country until 1866, when all the measuring systems in Romania were unified.

In towns and cities, open-air markets were often supplemented by the central bazaar, where traders and shopkeepers rented small retail units to sell their wares. Some bazaars or *suq*s like the one shown here consisted of partly covered rows of shops on either side of a broad thoroughfare.

In traditional covered bazaars and *suq*s, specialised trades and retailers tended to draw together. For security reasons, jewellers’ shops were often found in the centre. Precious merchandise was kept locked away in cabinets and was only produced at a customer’s request.

The Great Khan of Damascus was built in the 18th century to house caravans from all over the region, carrying goods from as far away as China and those coming from further west through Mediterranean ports. Its central area combined shops on the ground floor with lodgings above.

The Grand Bazaar in Istanbul has housed thousands of artisans’ workshops and retail units for nearly six centuries. Its craftsmen and merchants were members of professional guilds and clustered together in those areas of the bazaar that were allocated to them.

The 19th-century Ottoman Suq al-Hamidiyya is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and about 9 metres wide, allowing for comfortable browsing and shopping. The origins of the site on which it was built go back to pre-Islamic times.

This map indicating the location of shops in the heart of 19th-century Beirut gives a good impression of the clustered traditional concentration of commercial units typical within the Middle Eastern urban fabric.

In Istanbul, as elsewhere, traditional retailing from shops open to the street continued well into the 19th century. However, increasingly, commercial hubs in major cities were transformed with Western-style shops – often aligned under arcaded passages along the main thoroughfares – replacing old-style retail units.

Traditionally, Middle Eastern communities knew a retailer’s goods and quality through experience and word of mouth. Western-style advertising only arrived in the 19th century. Here, right next to the historical Bab Bhar in Tunis, a shop uses billboards to attract customers from across the square.

Founded by two Austro-Hungarian Jews, Leon Orosdi and Hermann Back, the luxurious Western-style Orosdi-Back department stores first opened in Cairo in 1856. Others branches soon followed all over the region. Unlike traditional shops, Orosdi-Back stores had fixed prices and did not allow bargaining.

This European-style furniture store in the heart of 19th-century Tunis was established by Eugenio and Alfredo Coen, two Jewish brothers from Livorno, Italy. Although the brothers made their home in Tunis, like other non-Muslim expatriates they maintained close networks and links with their community across the region and back home.

Many traditional professions throughout the Middle East suffered in the wake of cheap, high-quality products being imported into the region from Europe. Traditional local foods and drinks, however, continued to enjoy popularity regardless and still do so today.

In the 18th and early 19th centuries, the official imperial coinage of the Ottoman empire was legal tender in all of its provinces, including the Balkans. The circulation of Ottoman coins dominated the money markets in Romania, Moldovia and Wallachia.

In the Middle East as well as across the Red and Arabian seas, the Arab-Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean, the Maria Theresa thaler was highly regarded and used in all aspects of life – from dowry payments and jewellery to economic transactions. Muslim pilgrims, too, favoured this internationally accepted coin.

In the later 19th century, the London Stock Exchange became the world’s most powerful financial centre. By 1914, one-third of the public capital available to investors anywhere in the world was listed and traded on the London Stock Exchange. Other European powers tried to establish rival institutions, but none could match it in scale, scope or available resources.
